problem: Existing robot-centric datasets (CODa, SIT, JRDB) cover perception, detection and tracking but lack language and step-by-step reasoning annotations, so they cannot support interpretable vision-language navigation for quadruped robots.
motivation: Interpretable, human-like navigation needs explicit intermediate reasoning that links perception, language and action. Autonomous-driving work (DriveVLM, AlphaDrive) shows CoT helps planning, but no robot-perspective dataset provides such traces for indoor and outdoor pedestrian-area navigation.
key_idea: Build a large real-world Go2 quadruped dataset with GPT-4.1-generated, human-corrected four-step CoT VQA annotations, and fine-tune a Qwen2.5-VL-7B model (CoT-VLN) to reason before predicting 3-second waypoints.
insight: Both reasoning and vision matter: on average, removing CoT raises L2 error by about 8.8% (Qwen2.5-VL: 0.29 m with CoT vs 0.33 m without), and language-only models are worst (0.39 m for Qwen2.5-VL). Structured CoT with a discrete Servo/Path multiple-choice step makes trajectories more accurate than direct regression. The VLM also beats non-VLM driving planners (SparseDrive, DiffusionPlanner), which the authors attribute to more flexible open-world path selection.
method: Data collection: a wheeled Unitree Go2 with a Hesai XT32 Lidar, five 150° surround cameras at 10 Hz and IMU/GNSS; 60 scenes of 300 s each, indoor and outdoor, ~175K frames and 875K images

Annotations: 3D boxes with object IDs (Car, Bus, Bicycle, Pedestrian, Half-body, Cone) within 30 m at native 10 Hz; GNSS+IMU+SLAM localization; meta states Servo (Keep/Accelerate/Decelerate/Stop) and Path (Right Turn/Left Turn/Straight/IDLE)

Four-step CoT VQA pipeline: Environmental Perception, Key Agents Analysis (with distance and location), Walking Decision Reasoning (multiple-choice Servo/Path status), Trajectory Prediction Output; GPT-4.1 generates each step, then rule-based and manual correction
Input format: OmniDrive-style stitching of the front-left/front-right views and of the rear-left/rear/rear-right views
CoT-VLN model: Qwen2.5-VL-7B with frozen image encoder; projector and LLM trained with SFT on the CoT VQA data, with a 'think' trigger keyword; outputs 6 waypoints at 0.5 s intervals over 3 s
Evaluation protocol: open-loop L2 error at 1/2/3 s and average, plus GPT-4.1-as-judge scoring (1-100) of reasoning quality; 140K train / 35K val split

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-7B (fine-tuned, SFT; vision encoder frozen); baselines InternVL3-8B, Janus-Pro-7B, LLaVA-1.6-7B
setting.training_data: CoT-VLNBench train split: 140K VQA instances (80%) from own Go2 data, with GPT-4.1-generated and human-corrected CoT
setting.observation: five surround-view RGB cameras (stitched into two images) plus Lidar in the dataset; the VLM uses images only
setting.action_space: future waypoints: 6 (x,y) points over 3 s at 0.5 s intervals, plus discrete Servo/Path status
setting.simulator: real world only (offline dataset, open-loop evaluation)
setting.privileged: none at test time (3D box labels are used only to build the CoT annotations)

numbers.extra: SFT on the CoT-VLNBench train split with CoT reasoning; open-loop evaluation

numbers_note: Own benchmark, not a standard VLN benchmark; open-loop trajectory L2 errors only, no SR/SPL. Other trained variants exist in Table 2 and were not all listed.
results: CoT-VLN (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) reaches 0.29 m average L2 error, the best of the four VLMs (InternVL3-8B 0.31), and beats the non-VLM planners SparseDrive (0.42) and DiffusionPlanner (0.37). CoT reasoning gives about 8.8% lower error than non-reasoning, and removing vision gives worse results.
limitations: Only open-loop L2 evaluation on the authors' own data; no closed-loop navigation, success rate or standard VLN benchmark comparison

CoT annotations are generated by GPT-4.1, so they may inherit its errors, and the GPT-4.1 judge is subjective; instructions are largely a fixed 'What is your moving plan?' prompt rather than diverse language instructions
Dataset is small in scene count (60 scenes, 5 hours) and mostly urban pedestrian areas, and is not clearly released; inconsistent statistics in the paper (3.5M vs 5.25M boxes, 8.75M language pairs)
